quote: to getting fat, to getting fewer dates, to reproducing less successfully
content: In the one large dataset where this has been measured, the sign is reversed. Analysing three generations of the Framingham Heart Study, Byars and colleagues found that natural selection in a contemporary American population favoured women who were heavier, as well as shorter and with lower cholesterol, with the trends projected to continue (Byars et al. 2010). Reviews of selection in modern humans find it ongoing and measurable, and not in the direction the essay's causal chain assumes (Stearns et al. 2010). The essay's point that the taste bud does not track present fitness survives; the illustrative chain of consequences it offers is empirically backwards.

quote: Fifty thousand years ago, the taste buds of Homo sapiens directed their bearers to the scarcest, most critical food resources—sugar and fat.
content: Sweet receptors are not a hominin adaptation to Pleistocene scarcity; the TAS1R sweet/umami receptor family predates mammals and its evolution across vertebrates tracks diet in ways that have nothing to do with human famine (Shi & Zhang 2006). Nor is it established that ancestral humans were chronically calorie-limited: Hadza foragers expend no more energy per day than Westerners and remain lean, which points to intake and food environment rather than to a scarcity-tuned appetite as the modern problem (Pontzer et al. 2012). The "Adam liked sugar and ate an apple, 2763 generations later" story is a parable, and the essay should say so instead of dating it.

quote: No human being with the deliberate goal of maximizing their alleles’ inclusive genetic fitness would ever eat a cookie unless they were starving.
content: This is not obvious and the essay does not argue it. A deliberate fitness-maximiser in a modern food environment would eat cookies whenever their marginal fitness cost is negligible, which for most people most of the time it is; obesity's effect on reproductive success is small, sex-dependent, and in at least one large cohort positive for women (Byars et al. 2010). The sentence works rhetorically by importing an implicit model in which any sub-optimal calorie is a fitness loss, and it is the same implicit model that generated the thrifty-gene hypothesis, which has not survived genomic scrutiny (Ayub et al. 2014). The slogan that organisms are adaptation-executers is sound; the cookie example is just another adaptationist intuition.
